title: The night of the spirit
hook: a deeper night, where even our ideas of God are purified

segments.voice: Yesterday, three signs to tell the night of the senses from drifting or illness. Your line was the longing stays. Today, John says there's a second, deeper night.

A kind old man on a cloud. A stern one. A very large grandfather, or a referee with a whistle. Those are pictures of God a child might draw, and a child can outgrow them. But John of the Cross says grown-ups carry pictures of God too: God as my cheerleader, God as a rule book, God as the one who'll make my life work out. And he says there's a night in which even those get taken away.
screen: `A MAN ON A CLOUD.` → `GROWN-UP PICTURES OF GOD.` → `A NIGHT THAT TAKES THEM AWAY.`

segments.voice: First, who it's for. John says the night of the senses is common, and the night of the spirit is for fewer people, those who have already come a long way in prayer. It goes deeper. The first night weaned us from sweet feelings. This one reaches our understanding, our memory and our will, the very ways we think about God. Second, the ray of darkness. Look straight at the sun and you see nothing. You're blinded, not by too little light, but by too much. So when God's light strikes a soul that isn't ready for it, John says, it feels like darkness. He borrows a phrase from an older Christian writer, Dionysius: a ray of darkness. Third, the pain. John doesn't soften this. People in this night can feel abandoned, dry, even rejected by God, like the writer of Lamentations sitting in the ruins. Their old ideas of God don't hold up anymore, and nothing has taken their place yet. It's frightening. John says it's also love: God is making room for himself, the real God, not our picture. Fourth, bigger than your idea. The prophet Isaiah hears God say, in the Douay-Rheims: "For my thoughts are not your thoughts: nor your ways my ways, saith the Lord." Any idea of God we can hold in our heads, John says, is smaller than God. That doesn't make the ideas useless; the Church's teaching still stands. But the God it points to is always larger. Losing a picture, for John, isn't losing God. It can be finding him.
screen: `A DEEPER NIGHT, FOR FEWER.` · `A RAY OF DARKNESS.` · `THE OLD PICTURES DON'T HOLD.` · `GOD IS ALWAYS LARGER.` · then, large: `MY THOUGHTS ARE NOT YOUR THOUGHTS.`

segments.voice: Notice one picture of God you carry: the referee, the distant boss, the one who's disappointed in you, the one who owes you a good life. Just see it, then gently set it down, without rushing to replace it. If you pray, simply say, you're more than this; if you don't, hold the idea that whatever is deepest is larger than your picture of it.
Isaiah. The prophet John quotes for this deeper night, where God says his thoughts are not our thoughts, and even our ideas of God are purified. Today's word.
Your line: bigger than your idea. No picture holds all of God. Day two hundred sixty-three, done.

howItsDone: Catholics who experience long seasons of spiritual darkness are often pointed to the second book of John's Dark Night, usually with an experienced spiritual director, and the Church remembers saints such as Thérèse of Lisieux who described similar nights.
